experiencing back pain radiating to the chest.  At some point
the patient had a syncopal episode and fell onto her face.
The patient reports a positive loss of consciousness.  The
patient was found down, bleeding significantly from her face
and was brought immediately to the Emergency Department for
further evaluation.  Patient was normotensive in the 70s and
receiving intravenous fluids when she arrived at the
Emergency Department.  She was intubated in the Emergency
Department using Vecuronium and succinylcholine and was then
evaluated using many radiographic modalities which showed
multiple facial fractures.  The patient was then transferred
to the Trauma Surgical Intensive Care Unit for further
evaluation.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
1.  Osteoporosis.
2.  Compression fractures.

PAST SURGICAL HISTORY:  None.

MEDICATIONS:
1.  Fosamax.
2.  Aspirin.

ALLERGIES:  No known drug allergies.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION:  On arrival her temperature is 100.8,
pulse of 74, blood pressure 146/68, 14, 100%.  The initial
settings for the respirator are IMV at a tidal volume 500,
rate of 14, FIO2 60%, and peak of 5.  In general, intubated,
sedated, paralyzed.  HEENT:  Traumatic facial fractures with
skull depression.  Bilateral tympanic membranes without
blood.  Pupils pinpoint, sluggish to light. Neck:  In collar
without LAD or jugular venous distention.  Carotids 2+.
Rectal:  Guaiac negative, decreased tone.  Lungs:  Clear to
auscultation bilaterally.  Heart is regular rate and rhythm;
normal S1 and S2.  Abdomen:  Soft, nontender, nondistended;
no hepatosplenomegaly.  Extremities: Upper extremity full
range of passive; left lower extremity full range of movement
in passive motion; 1+ pitting edema bilateral knees.

dorsalis pedis all 2+.

15, hematocrit of 30, and platelet count of 206.  CK was 119,
troponin was less than 0.01.  Urinalysis was negative.
Urinary electrolytes were unremarkable.

the Trauma SICU, where she was evaluated by Ear, Nose, and
Throat as well as Plastics for the facial fractures and
epistaxis.  The ENT service at this point used balloons to
tamponade the bleeding from the patient's nose.  Multiple
adjustments were made during the Trauma SICU time in order to
control the bleeding.  The initial evaluation by Plastic
Surgery was that the patient would require in-house surgical
repair of the multiple fractures.

After a short stay in the Trauma SICU the patient was then
evaluated by Cardiology, who determined that the patient
either had sick sinus syndrome or another intermittent
arteriovenous block or block below the AV node which
resulted in four- to five-second pauses on telemetry
monitoring.  The Cardiology service felt the best course of
action was to place a pacemaker for the patient.  This
procedure was done without complication.  The patient was
extubated and after a short period of time was sent to the
Trauma Floor for further evaluation and possible surgical
repair of facial fractures.

After a short time on the floor patient was reevaluated by
the Plastic Surgery service, who felt that at this point her
facial fractures were non-operative.  The ENT service also
felt that the epistaxis was under control and that no other
intervention was necessary.  The patient was evaluated by
Speech and Swallow and Physical Therapy, and it was
determined that the patient would leave the hospital to go to
rehab prior to going home to ensure the patient's safety.  At
time of discharge the patient had improving pain symptoms and
was improving overall clinically.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:  Good.

DISPOSITION:  To rehab.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:
1.  Syncope.
2.  Pacemaker placement.
3.  Multiple facial fractures.
4.  Likely repaired intermittent arteriovenous block or block
below the arteriovenous node.

DISCHARGE MEDICATIONS:
1.  Percocet 325.
2.  Colace 100 b.i.d.
3.  Erythromycin ointment, one to two drops ophthalmic q.i.d.
4.  Famotidine q. 12 hours.
5.  Bisacodyl 10 mg suppository q. h.s.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
1.  Follow up with the Trauma Clinic in one to two weeks.
2.  Follow up with the [**Hospital 3595**] Clinic in one to two weeks.
3.  The patient may also follow up with her outpatient
plastic surgeon, Dr. [**First Name (STitle) **], for possible repair of the
fractures in the future.

Degloving injury of the scalp.

Hypertension.

Hypercholesterolemia.

   HPI:  This is an 81 year old female with a complicated past medical

   course uncomplicated, received 2 units PRBCs in OR.  Post-operatively
   has been easily arousable but became disoriented and non-verbal so was
   transferred to medicine yesterday ([**4-2**]).
   .
   Her U/A was c/w UTI, so the patient was started on cipro. Overnight, pt
   desatted to 61% on RA, improved to 93% on NRB.  CXR was c/w pulm edema,
   and she was diuresed with lasix 20mg IV with improvement in O2sats to
   80s-90s on 3-4L; reliable O2sats were difficulty to obtain as pt moving
   around a lot and was pulling off mask. She was diuresed again today
   with lasix 20mg IV with a total UOP of 3L from both lasix doses.  Her
   ucx grew out cipro-resistent proteus this afternoon, so she was
   switched to ceftriaxone.  Her mental status seemed marginally improved
   today, responding to name and intermittently to simple qustions.
   .
   In the late afternoon, she once again desatted to 70s on 3L. ABG at
   that time was 7.54/31/44.  She was placed on a 100% NRB with
   improvement in ABG to 7.49/35/65.  CXR appeared stable.  EKG unchanged;
   cardiac enzymes with nl CK and trop 0.04. Given her rising WBC to 25
   today (in setting of suboptimal UTI tx) and respiratory decompensation,
   she was started empirically on vancomycin and cefepime for possible
   HCAP. She appeared a little more stable with O2sats in high 90s on NRB
   so was tried on 50% FM with O2sats 84-85%.  She was given an additional
   dose of lasix 20mg IV. Given her AMS and high aspiration risk, it was
   thought that she would not tolerate bipap.  Per extensive family
   discussion was maintained DNR but ok to intubate, so she was
   transferred to the MICU for further monitoring in the setting of

[**9-7**] pain in the left leg after falling and called for her

reduction/internal fixation was initially delayed secondary
to her elevated INR.

After correction of her INR, the patient went for open
reduction/internal fixation.  This was complicated by some
hypotension intraoperatively with induction.  The patient was
given multiple liters of intravenous fluids, after which the
patient could not be extubated secondary to hypoxemia and
hypercarbic respiratory failure; likely secondary to
congestive heart failure with aggressive intravenous fluid
hydration.

The patient was admitted to the Medical Intensive Care Unit
for a transient 3-day stay, where she was diuresed with
Lasix.  The patient's respiratory failure improved markedly.
She was extubated and remained on the floor with a chest
x-ray showing some resolving atelectasis and pneumonia.

ejection fraction of 60% with some evidence of diastolic
dysfunction.

The patient was continued on ceftriaxone and azithromycin for

aggressive fluid resuscitation in the operating room.

stable oxygen saturations on the floor.

creatinine of 1.3 to 1.6 which peaked to 2.2 postoperatively.

1%, this may be secondary to acute tubular necrosis from
operative hypotension.  The patient's creatinine on the floor
subsequently improved to 1.4 (at her baseline).

5.  PULMONARY EMBOLISM ISSUES:  The patient has a history of
a recent pulmonary embolism, for which she was started on
Coumadin.  No clear etiology for her pulmonary embolism.  The
patient was continued on Coumadin postoperatively.

6.  ORTHOPAEDIC ISSUES:  The patient with a left spiral
tibia/fibula fracture, status post open reduction/internal
fixation.  The patient's wound on the floor looked to be

DISCHARGE STATUS:  The patient was to be discharged to a

TEXT:
58 year old man admitted via the ed last night with hypotension
   likely r/t bacteremic vs hypovolemic shock. The pt presented to his
   usual dialysis treatment and was found to be hypotensive with sbp <50
   during his dialysis run. He refused transfer to the hospital and,
   following a conversation with his hepatologist.
      Overnight, the pt received aggressive fluid resuscitation including
   4 units prbc
s and 3 liters ivf. INR was reversed with 4 units of
   plasma as well. Received the pt on maximum levophed dosing and
   2mcgs/kg/min of neo as well. An arterial line and right femerol cordis
   were in place.
   Events Today: A left subclavian triple lumen catheter was placed in ir.
   The team is aware and will remove the femerol cordis this evening.
   While in the ir suite, a diagnostic and therapeutic paracentesis was
   performed. Cultures were sent to r/o sbp and 7 liters were removed from
   his abdomen. The patient received 175gms of albumin during and after
   the paracentesis. The patient was later weaned from the neo drip.
   Hypotension (not Shock)
   Assessment:
   As noted above, the neo drip was weaned off this afternoon and the
   levophed drip is slowly being titrated down to maintain maps >60. He
   has not received any additional ivf. He remains on abx coverage for a
   suspected sbp. Pt has been afebrile this afternoon with a lactate level
   trending downward.
   Action:
   Actively weaning pressor support s/p albumin infusion.
   Response:
   Pt tolerating pressor wean thus far.
   Plan:
   Monitor hemodynamic status closely and titrate pressors as pt
   tolerates. Continue to monitor temperature curve and give abx as
   ordered. Follow up with culture data.
   Anemia, acute, secondary to blood loss (Hemorrhage, Bleeding)
   Assessment:
   Serial hct results are trending downward this afternoon: 29->26->22. Pt
   has had two grossly bloody stools following laculose dosing this
   morning. He has been seen by the liver team and will have a flex
   sigmoidoscopy tomarrow.
   Action:
   Serial hcts trending downward.
   Response:
   Pt has had no additional bleeding since this morning in the setting of
   receiving lactulose.
   Plan:
   Follow up with the micu team re: additional blood transfusions.
   Continue lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy. Per liver team, please
   give tap water enemas x2 in the morning and anticipate flex sig
   tomarrow. NPO after mn
   Renal failure, End stage (End stage renal disease, ESRD)
   Assessment:
   Per discussion with the renal fellow, there is no immediate need for
   dialysis, uremia is stable and lytes are within acceptable range. The
   fellow did have a discussion with the patient re: line placement (pt is
   dialyzed via a left arm graft and would need a venous access for crrt)
   which the pt is currently refusing. Pt does have significant lower
   extremity edema which he reports is more chronic than acute.
   Action:
   None; will hold off on dialysis today and likely again tomorrow then
   reassess. Hopefully, the pt will be more hemodynamically stable for HD.
   Response:
   Plan:
   Follow serial lytes with renal function. Monitor volume status closely.
   Pain control (acute pain, chronic pain)
   Assessment:
   Pt has c/o acute abdominal, left shoulder, and leg pain today. He
   states that he takes [**4-14**] oxycodones daily for chronic pain relief.
   Following a clear liquid breakfast, the pt c/o acute, intense [**11-20**]
   abdominal pain. He received a single dose of oxycodone w/o effect. The
   micu resident was called to evaluate the pt and he subsequently
   received a total of 4mg ivp morphine with modest improvement in pain
   ([**9-20**]). The pt received additional doses of versed and fentanyl during
   his ir stay.
   Action:
   Pt has received multiple doses of narcotics with minimal to modest
   relief from pain.
   Response:
   Pt returned from ir and has been napping for much of the remaining
   shift. He is easily arousable and oriented.
   Plan:
   Monitor pain control. Give analgesia as pt tolerates.

s and falling Hct,
   labs concerning for DIC vs hemolysis, multifocal PNA
s on chest CT.
   .
   # Hypotension/shock. Pt remains on Levophed and Midodrine and we have
   been limited in our ability to wean Levophed.  Our initial thought was
   that the hypotension was due to sepsis from a pulmonary source, based
   on CT scan.  We are giving Vanc/Cefepime/Cipro for PNA and Flagyl to
   cover possible intraabdominal source given colitis on CT scan.  With
   his dilated, hypokinetic RV on echo, another possibility would be poor
   cardiac output secondary to fluid overload causing RV dilatation.  He
   could be preload dependent and not getting enough output from his right
   ventricle.  Negative paracentesis. CvO2 77%.  No PE on CTA.  Mycoplasma
   IgM negative.
   - Talk to renal about doing ultrafiltration between dialysis days to
   have more fluid removed.
   - Cefepime and Vanc are day [**8-17**], Cipro and Flagyl day [**7-18**], Tamiflu are
   day [**6-15**]
   - Increase midodrine to 10mg TID so that levophed can hopefully be
   weaned further.
   - Infectious work-up negative to date.
   - We will hold off on R heart cath / Cards consult to assess the
   physiology of his R heart failure for now as this would probably not
   change management.
   - No IVF's for today
   .
   # GIB/anemia. Pt having intermittently bloody BM's, with stable Hct.
   Likely source was hemorrhoids given rectal pain.  No plan for
   sigmoidoscopy by hepatology for the time being.  Other differential
   includes ischemic colitis (with hypotension from other etiology),
   diverticulosis, hemorrhoids, AVMs, polyps.
   - Continue to follow daily Hct and coags, fibrinogen and platelets
   - Heme feels that significant hemolysis and DIC are unlikely, but
   suggest following daily DIC labs.
   - If acute bleed, needs to go to bleeding scan
   .
    # Mental status: Pt seen to be occasionally confused, saying odd
   things, and sometimes belligerent, making aggressive/rude comments to
   staff, and other times non-compliant, taking off BP cuff, pressing the
   pump buttons, not staying in bed, etc. Could be related to hepatic
   encephalopathy vs personality disorder.
   - Psych consult
   - Currently getting PO Lactulose, but has been intermittently refusing.
   - Start TID rifaximin 400mg.
   .
   # Right heart failure: Patient has right heart failure on echo without
   evidence of extreme pulmonary hypertension.  No PE seen on CTA.  This
   is new from [**2142**].  Possibilities include severe fluid overload (off
   starling curve) or old infarct.  It would be useful to get him drier to
   see if his RV function improves.  He had 3.5L off during dialysis
   today, but it will be difficult to make him significantly negative with
   QOD dialysis.  We would prefer to do ultrafiltration on non-dialysis
   days to get more fluid off.
   - f/u whether he could get ultrafiltration today
   - can consider another paracentesis for fluid removal.
   - Could consider swan-ganz catheter or vigileo for clearer
   interpretation of heart function.
   .
   # ESRD.  On HD Tu/[**Doctor First Name **]/Sat as outpatient, but here plan is HD as needed
   based on fluid and electrolyte status. Had HD on Friday, Saturday and
   today.
   - f/u renal recs.
   - vanco dosed after dialysis.
   .
   # Abdominal pain/colitis.  Concerning for colitis on CT scan vs. bowel
   wall edema with total body anasarca.  C diff negative
   - flagyl for colitis as above
   .
   # Low cortisol
 continue stress-dosed steroids with fludrocort and
   hydrocort.  Plan to wean once blood pressures improved.
   .
   # Cirrhosis.  LFTs relatively at baseline (bili slightly up compared to
   prior).  Mental status surprisingly good considering blood pressure -
   no current evidence of hepatic encephalopathy, though would be at risk
   with GIB.
   - monitor mental status
   - Lactulose and rifaximin
   - Liver following.
   .
   # Elevated Troponin
 troponin stabilized.  Was likely demand ischemia,
   pt without current chest pain

transferred from an outside hospital.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  The patient is a 56-year-old
male with complex past medical history including fistulizing
with ileostomy.  He also had a history of chronic lymphocytic
leukemia which was diagnosed in the setting of Remicade use,
ankylosing spondylitis which was led to a mild restrictive lung
disease.  He has had additional congestive obstructive
pulmonary disease.

He has been seen in the past at [**First Name (Titles) **]
[**Last Name (Titles) 1029**] at an outside hospital approximately one month
ago for increasing lower extremity edema.  He was seen there
by their Pulmonary Service, and thought to have restrictive
lung disease greater than congestive obstructive pulmonary
disease with a gas in the setting in some sort of congestive
obstructive pulmonary disease exacerbation of 7.2/70/70.  He
was discharged on 2 liters of oxygen to rehabilitation.

He was doing well at rehabilitation, although he was put on
prednisone 60 mg q day for further obstructive
pulmonary disease exacerbation at an unknown date in the
rehabilitation.  He was found at the rehab to have a dropping
hematocrit.  He then was found to have a hematocrit drop from
30 to 20 with small blood in the ileostomy bag.  He was
returned to the outside hospital, where the night prior to
admission he was found to have 700 cc of frank blood and
clots in his ostomy bag.  Blood pressure was in the 70's,
heart rate in the 100's.  He received 6 units of packed red
blood cells and 2 units of fresh-frozen plasma, 2 units of
platelets, and fluid resuscitated briefly on Levophed.  He
was intubated for airway protection.  He also had a normal
esophagogastroduodenoscopy at the outside hospital.  He was
transferred here for further workup.

2. Klonopin 0.5 mg tid.
3. Ativan 0.5 mg prn.
4. Protonix 40 mg po q day.
5. Prednisone 40 mg q day.
6. Albuterol inhaler.
7. Atrovent inhaler.
8. Trazodone 50 mg q hs.
9. Allopurinol 300 mg q day.
10. Coumadin.

ALLERGIES:  Penicillin and sulfa.

SOCIAL HISTORY:  Has past heavy tobacco use, quit in [**9-17**].
History of alcohol abuse.  He is a [**Country 3992**] Veteran.  He lives
at home with his wife and daughter.

FAMILY HISTORY: Unobtainable at the time of admission to the
ICU.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
1. Congestive obstructive pulmonary disease on 2 liters home
O2.
2. History of restrictive lung disease secondary to
ankylosing spondylitis.
3. Fistulizing Crohn's disease status post partial colectomy
and ileectomy with ileostomy.
4. Chronic lymphocytic leukemia plus splenomegaly with
sequestration.
5. Depression.
6. Bilateral lower extremity edema.
7. Ankylosing spondylitis.
8. Pulmonary hypertension secondary to his chronic lung
disease which has led to some degree of right heart failure.
9. Thrombocytopenia which is secondary to splenic
sequestration in the setting of chronic lymphocytic leukemia.
10. Coronary artery disease, not further specified.
11. Hypertension.

PHYSICAL EXAM ON ADMISSION:  Vital signs:  Temperature of
100, heart rate of 102, blood pressure 113/60, respiratory
rate on SIMV with a rate of 10, sating 100%.  General:
Normocephalic, atraumatic, intubated, alert, and responsive
nonverbally, moving all four limbs appropriately.
Extraocular movements are intact.  Pupils are equal and
reactive to light.  Cardiovascular:  Regular, rate, and
rhythm, S1, S2, [**2-19**] holosystolic murmur.  Respiratory:  Clear
to auscultation anteriorly.  Abdomen is soft, nontender,
bowel sounds present, multiple scars right ileostomy.
Extremities:  [**12-18**]+ lower extremity edema, no rashes and no
icterus.

LABORATORY VALUES ON ADMISSION:  White blood cell count of
17, hematocrit of 28.6, and platelets of 60.  Sodium of 142,
potassium of 4.5, chloride 105, bicarb of 30, BUN 48,
creatinine 0.9, glucose 121, albumin 2.7.  Calcium,
magnesium, phosphorus of 7.9, 1.3, and 3.6.  INR of 1.0.

ELECTROCARDIOGRAM:  An electrocardiogram showed normal sinus
rhythm, normal intervals, normal axis, no ST-T wave changes.

CHEST X-RAY:  Showed bibasilar atelectasis and a small
pleural effusion, no pneumothorax.

An arterial blood gas on admission showed 7.47/47/50 on a
FIO2 of 40% and a PEEP of 5.

HOSPITAL COURSE TO DATE:  1. The patient was brought in,
intubated, and partially sedated.  His stool was guaiac
positive, but there was no frank blood.  Hematocrit was
stable at 28.  An esophagogastroduodenoscopy had already been
done at an outside hospital, and decision was made not to
repeat the study as it was negative.

He was prepped for a scope proximal from his ileostomy.
Surgery was also consulted.  As patient's hematocrit was
stable, and the ileostomy site scope was normal, further
intervention was deferred.  The patient was kept on a
proton-pump inhibitor.

In the setting of changing his ileostomy bag, an arterial
bleed was opened up from the skin connection from his
ileostomy at the surgical site.  This was tied off by the
MICU intern.  Since that time, he has had no further bleed.
Ileostomy output is sporadically guaiac positive.  No frank
blood.  Hematocrit has been stable.  It is felt that GI bleed
was secondary to this arterial lesion, which was probably a
surgical site ulcer.

2. Sepsis:  The patient was brought in febrile and
hypotensive.  On sputum culture, he was found to have 4+
Strep pneumoniae, and where he had been on 25 PMNs, he was
started on antibiotics for this.  Sensitivities returned late
in the course after receiving Vancomycin and ceftriaxone, and
levofloxacin.  The Strep pneumoniae happened to be resistant
to levofloxacin and intermediate sensitivity to ceftriaxone.
It was sensitive to erythromycin.  It was switched to
azithromycin and the patient recovered well late in the
hospitalization with blood pressures stabilizing off pressors
and becoming afebrile with a white blood cell count
decreasing from a peak in the 30's to 6.7.  No other
infectious processes were found during this hospitalization.

3. Respiratory:  Patient was initially brought in intubated
from the outside hospital.  On the second day of
hospitalization, he was briefly extubated, but became
tachypneic and had a hypercarbic respiratory dysfunction despite
non-invasive ventilation, requiring reintubation.  He remained
intubated until [**2105-3-6**] when after a very slow weaning process,
it was felt that his clinical condition had improved to the point
that he would tolerate extubation well.

He also on CT scan, was found to have a large bilateral
pleural effusions.  An ultrasound was performed and there was
only a small left pleural effusion which was not tapped, however,
the right pleural effusion was tapped which removed 600 cc of
serosanguinous transudative effusion.  Removal of this also
likely helped his pulmonary function to the point where he
could be extubated.  He was extubated uneventfully, and was
maintained well on decreasing amounts of ventilation
originally on BiPAP, and then switched to a face mask, and to
2 liters nasal cannula with goal oxygen saturations in the
low 90%.

It is assumed that this patient's normal pCO2 is in the 50's
as he has chronic lung disease.

4. Heme:  The patient has known chronic lymphocytic leukemia
with thrombocytopenia.  His platelets remain stable within
the 60-80 range.  He was not transfused any platelets during
this admission.  He did require multiple transfusions to
maintain his hematocrit above 28 in the setting of congestive
obstructive pulmonary disease and coronary artery disease.
He is a difficult crossmatch, however, transfusions proceeded
without complication.  He was also given 40,000 units of epo
for a low retic count.

His Allopurinol was held, it was an unclear indication,
probable gout.  He was also taken off Coumadin.  There was no
clear indication for Coumadin.  Best we can learn from
records was that he was started for feeling of a high risk
for deep venous thrombosis due to his underlying diseases.

5. Renal:  The patient developed acute renal failure with a
peak creatinine of 2.3, and urine sediment with multiple
white blood cells.  It was felt that this renal failure was
secondary to a combination of prerenal failure with an amount
of ATN as well as AIN from the ceftriaxone.  Ceftriaxone was
discontinued and as pressures were normalized, the patient's
creatinine and renal function improved, and urine output
improved as well.  The patient was transiently put on calcium
carbonate for phosphorus control as was phosphorus was
elevated during his renal failure.

6. FEN:  The patient was kept on tube feeds while intubated
and advanced to a po diet prior to transfer to the floor.

7. Prophylaxis:  He was kept on pneumoboots, proton-pump
inhibitor, and subQ Heparin throughout hospitalization.

8. Cardiovascular:  Aside from the initial need for pressors
to maintain blood pressure, the patient's cardiovascular
status was stable throughout hospitalization.  There was no
signs of ischemic changes.  After the bleed was stabilized,
he was started on aspirin which was continued during the rest
of the hospitalization.  Heart rate was well controlled.
There are no other cardiovascular issues.

This dictation will be addended with discharge medications
prior to discharge by the floor team.

Ranitidine 150 mg p.o. b.i.d.
